listening.instructions: You will hear a conversation between two friends, Tom and Lena, about Lena's company. You will hear it twice. Choose the correct answer for each question.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: So, six months into the four-day week. Are you going to keep it?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: I think so, yes, although it wasn't the smooth ride I expected. The first month was chaotic. Clients kept emailing on Fridays and expecting answers straight away.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: How did you get round that?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: We split the team, so two people cover Fridays and take Mondays off instead. It sounds obvious now, but it took us a while to realise that a four-day week doesn't mean everyone has the same day off.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: And productivity? That's what everyone asks about.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Honestly, the amount of work we produce is about the same. What's changed is how we work. Meetings were the first thing to go. We used to have a two-hour planning meeting every Monday. Now it's twenty minutes, and we do it standing up.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: I'd have thought people would be more stressed, squeezing five days into four.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: That was my biggest worry before we started. And a couple of people did struggle at first. But sick days have dropped by almost half, and nobody has left the company this year, which in our industry is unusual.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: So it's really about keeping staff.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Partly. Recruiting a good designer costs us a fortune, so if people stay, that's a huge saving. But I'd be lying if I said it was purely about money. I wanted a business I'd actually enjoy running.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Would you recommend it to other companies?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Not to everyone. If your work depends on being available to customers all day, every day, like a shop, it's much harder. And you have to trust your staff. If a manager feels the need to check what people are doing every hour, it simply won't work.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: You make it sound like it's more about management than about hours.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: That's exactly it. Changing the hours just showed us habits we should have dropped years ago.

reading.passage:
The return of the night train

For most of the last thirty years, Europe's sleeper trains seemed to be heading for the museum. Cheap flights had made the overnight journey look slow and old-fashioned, and one by one, national rail companies cancelled routes that were losing money. By 2016, even the famous service between Paris and the Italian border had disappeared.

Today the picture looks very different. New routes have opened between cities such as Brussels and Berlin, Vienna and Amsterdam, and Zurich and Rome. Several of them sell out weeks in advance during the summer. So what has changed?

The most obvious answer is climate anxiety. A passenger travelling from Vienna to Paris by train produces a fraction of the carbon emissions of the same trip by plane, and a growing number of travellers say this matters to them. Yet operators are careful not to rely on good intentions alone. 'People may choose the train once to feel virtuous,' says Clara Weiss, who manages one of the new services. 'They come back because it is genuinely convenient.'

Convenience, in this case, is about time rather than speed. A flight from Brussels to Berlin takes just over an hour, but once you add the journey to the airport, security checks and the trip into the city at the other end, the total is closer to five. The night train takes eleven hours, but the passenger boards in the city centre after dinner and arrives in the morning, having slept for most of the journey. Many business travellers also point out that it saves them the cost of a hotel.

There are still serious obstacles. Sleeping cars are expensive to build and can only make one trip per day, so tickets are rarely as cheap as budget flights. Each country charges its own fees for using its tracks, and some routes cross four or five borders. Several operators have also struggled with old carriages which break down, leading to delays and angry reviews.

Weiss is nevertheless optimistic. She believes governments will eventually have to make rail travel cheaper compared with flying, whether through taxes on aviation fuel or support for rail companies. 'We are not trying to replace every flight,' she says. 'But for journeys of up to about a thousand kilometres, we think the train should be the natural choice. We are not there yet, but ten years ago nobody was even asking the question.'

reading.passage:
Bees on the roof

When Hannah Okafor put two beehives on the roof of her London office block five years ago, her colleagues thought she had lost her mind. [1] Today the building has twelve hives, a waiting list of staff who want to help, and its own brand of honey, which sells out every autumn.

Okafor is part of a boom in urban beekeeping. In some European cities, the number of registered hives has more than doubled in a decade. [2] Gardens, parks and even balconies offer a wider variety of flowers than many farms, where a single crop may cover hundreds of hectares and chemical sprays are common.

However, not everyone is delighted. Some scientists warn that the trend may be doing more harm than good. [3] Wild bees, of which there are hundreds of species, depend on the same flowers. If too many honeybee hives are placed in one area, the wild bees may simply not find enough food.

Okafor takes the criticism seriously. [4] Instead, her company now spends part of the money from honey sales on planting wildflowers in nearby streets and schools. 'If you want to help bees,' she says, 'plant things first and keep hives second.'

There are practical challenges, too. Hives need checking every week in spring and summer, and a strong wind on a rooftop can be dangerous for both bees and beekeeper. [5] For this reason, most city beekeeping associations now insist that beginners complete a course before they buy their first colony.

For Okafor, the greatest benefit has been unexpected. [6] 'People who had worked on different floors for years started talking to each other on the roof,' she says. 'The bees did more for our office than any team-building day.'

texts.title: Email from Priya
texts.body:
Hi Sam,

Three weeks in and I'm finally getting used to waking up at five! The turtle project is harder work than I imagined. We patrol the beach every night during nesting season, and I've been bitten by more insects than I can count. But last night we watched forty baby turtles reach the sea, and I honestly cried.

The other volunteers are mostly students, although there's a retired couple from Canada who are the fittest people here. My only complaint is the food. Rice and beans every single day. I'd do anything for a pizza.

Write soon,
Priya

texts.title: Advert: Global Hands
texts.body:
Make a difference this summer with Global Hands! We offer two to twelve-week placements in teaching, conservation and healthcare in over twenty countries. No experience is necessary. Every volunteer receives a full day of online training before departure and has a local coordinator available twenty-four hours a day.

Prices start at £950 for two weeks and include accommodation, meals and airport transfers. Flights are not included. Book before 31 March and receive a 10% discount. Volunteers must be aged eighteen or over.

texts.title: Article: Is voluntourism really helping?
texts.body:
Every year, thousands of well-meaning young people pay to spend a few weeks volunteering abroad. But critics argue that short placements can do real damage. Children in orphanages, for example, may become attached to a series of volunteers who then disappear. Building projects carried out by unskilled visitors sometimes have to be redone by local workers, who could have been paid to do the job in the first place.

That does not mean nobody should volunteer. Experts suggest choosing placements of at least three months, avoiding any work with young children, and asking organisations exactly how much of the fee reaches the local community.

texts.title: Review: Coastal Futures Trust
texts.body:
I spent six months with Coastal Futures Trust after finishing university, and I can't recommend them highly enough. Unlike some larger companies, they publish a full breakdown of where volunteers' money goes, and almost all the project leaders are local marine biologists.

The accommodation is basic, with shared rooms and cold showers, so it's not for everyone. But the training was excellent, and I've since used the experience to get a job in environmental research. My one criticism is that the office in the UK was slow to answer emails before I left.

reading.passage:
The woman who counted the birds

Edith Marlowe was born in 1921 in a small fishing village on the north-east coast of Scotland. Her father ran the village shop, and her mother taught at the local school, where Edith was a quiet pupil who preferred being outdoors to sitting at a desk. At the age of nine, she was given a pair of binoculars by her uncle, a sailor, and she began recording every bird she saw in a notebook she kept under her bed.

When she left school, there were few opportunities for young women in science. Edith worked for eleven years as a clerk at a shipping company in Aberdeen, spending every weekend walking along the cliffs. Over time, her notebooks became remarkably detailed. She recorded not only which species she saw, but also the weather, the time of day and how many birds were nesting.

In 1953, a professor from the University of Edinburgh happened to read a short letter she had written to a local newspaper about the decline of puffins on the coast. He contacted her and asked to see her records. He was astonished to find more than twenty years of careful observations, which nobody else had collected. With his support, she was given a part-time research post, and in 1961 she published her first book, Cliffs and Wings, which became an unexpected bestseller.

Edith's records later proved extremely valuable. In the 1980s, scientists studying the effect of rising sea temperatures used her data to show how seabird populations had changed over half a century. She was awarded an honorary degree in 1987, although she joked that she had 'never passed an exam in her life'.

She continued counting birds until she was eighty-five. When she died in 2009, she left all of her notebooks, more than three hundred of them, to the university, where they are still used by students today.
